clue.text: Type of novel ice, not scenic if cracked

indicators.note: Something cracked has broken apart, and pieces that have broken apart do not stay in the order they were laid out in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters, comma and all

explanation.surface: A novel set on ice that is nothing much to look at and has started to break up.
explanation.walkthrough: Fourteen letters of fodder is a lot to shuffle, so count them against the enumeration before you start. The comma after 'ice' is punctuation, and a setter is free to ignore it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Type of novel' asks for the name of a genre, and the answer is the genre of imagined technology, space travel and futures that have not happened.

clue.text: Determined effort to meet upstairs for massage

indicators.note: To massage figures is to work them over until they come out looking different, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: Two people arranging to meet upstairs for a massage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstairs' in a down clue looks like an instruction to run letters up the grid towards the top. It is fodder, and every word after the definition goes into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A determined effort is a try made in earnest: the first word of the answer carries 'determined', the second carries 'effort', both as plain synonyms.

clue.text: Unsophisticated member enthralled by trendy European worker

indicators.note: To be enthralled is to be held captive, so the captive word sits inside the words that are holding it.

parts.note: in = fashionable, trendy
standard abbreviation
the worker of crosswords is the ant
a member is a limb

explanation.surface: An unpolished club member being captivated by a fashionable European colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is the ant of a thousand crosswords and 'member' is a limb rather than a person. Two disguises worth owning, because setters reach for both every week.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: 'unsophisticated' and the answer both describe a person or thing that lacks polish, grace and social finish.

clue.text: Press's outspoken demands

indicators.note: Outspoken splits into 'out spoken' — said aloud — so this word is handed to you by its sound rather than its spelling.

parts.note: to press dough is to knead it, so 'presses' is 'kneads', whose opening K is silent

explanation.surface: The newspapers being blunt about what they want.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is a verb ending, not a possessive: 'press's' is 'presses'. Bakers press dough under another name, and that name starts with a letter you never hear.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Demands' is the plural noun here — the things somebody must have — and the answer is the everyday word for requirements of that kind.

clue.text: Skin rash oddly deep, I'm starting to itch, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the collected letters are put out of order
oddly means taking the odd-numbered letters, the first and third

parts.note: its first and third letters are taken
taken as written
taken as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: starting to points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A patient complains of a deep rash on their skin that is beginning to itch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' gives RS from 'rash' and 'starting to' gives I from 'itch'; with DEEP and IM these nine letters are rearranged, as 'unfortunately' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin, so it can stand for skin itself.

clue.text: See 1
Type of food (French) that is delicious starter

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective while 'type of food' is a noun phrase; a menu names a category this way, calling a dish by the method that cooked it.

parts.note: standard abbreviation
i.e. = that is

indicators.note: A starter is whatever comes first, so the letter taken is the one that starts the word beside it.

parts.note: the first letter of delicious

explanation.surface: A French dish that is a delicious way to begin a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' is Latin i.e. in disguise, one of the small workhorses of this language. The brackets round 'French' are the setter flagging an abbreviation rather than making an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Type of food' points at a whole class of dishes named by how they were cooked, which is the sense the answer carries on any menu.

clue.text: Guy with cape swallowing drug that 12 might like

definitions.note: This is a cross-reference rather than a synonym: 12 across's answer names a person, and this answer is the quality that person would welcome.

indicators.note: Swallowing takes something down inside you, so whatever gets swallowed ends up in the middle of the word doing the swallowing.

parts.note: a chap is a guy, a bloke
E is ecstasy, the crossword drug of choice
a ness is a headland — Sheerness, Orford Ness

explanation.surface: A man in a cape gulping down a pill.
explanation.walkthrough: The cape in the surface is the superhero kind, and in the wordplay it is coastline: a ness is a headland, which is how British setters clue 'cape' without leaving the country.
explanation.definitionFit: 12's answer is someone settling a bill, and low prices are what such a person hopes for — the answer is the noun for goods costing little.

clue.text: I can show one score, not 150

indicators.note: 'Not' is doing subtraction here: whatever follows it is taken back out of what has just been put together.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a running score is a tally
read it aloud as 'one fifty' — that is one L, since L is the Roman fifty, and one L comes out

explanation.surface: Somebody offering to produce a scoreline: one, not a hundred and fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: '150' is not a numeral to convert but a number to say out loud. One fifty is one L, and a single L is exactly what has to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: 'I' is the international vehicle registration letter carried by cars from this country, so the plate stands in for the country — definition by abbreviation.

clue.text: Maybe Cocaine's indicative of normal songs

definitions.note: 'Cocaine' is a single example offered with 'maybe', while the answer is plural: the clue points at a whole class by naming one member of it.

parts.note: normal = as nature made it, unforced
in showbusiness a song is a number — 'a lively number'

explanation.surface: Perhaps the song Cocaine tells you something about ordinary music.
explanation.walkthrough: Cocaine is set in italics because it is a title — the JJ Cale song Clapton made famous — and it is a song grown from a plant, which is the whole of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The italics make Cocaine a song title; a song is a number, and this one comes from a plant rather than a lab, so it qualifies by example.

clue.text: Ray meeting first lady magistrate

indicators.note: Two things that meet are set side by side, so these pieces are simply laid end to end in the order given.

parts.note: ray is the second note of the sol-fa scale, and setters spell it RE
the first lady of Genesis

explanation.surface: Ray is introduced to the first lady, who sits as a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: Doh, ray, me: the sol-fa scale is a standing source of two-letter chunks, and 'first lady' is the oldest one there is rather than a president's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the medieval English officer who kept order in a manor, town or shire, so 'magistrate' fits in its older administrative sense.

clue.text: Vagrant makes one point before shouting

indicators.note: 'Before' fixes the order: what has been named ahead of it goes in front of what is named after it.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a tine is the point of a fork or an antler
to rant is to shout on and on

explanation.surface: A drifter gets one argument in before the shouting starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like a compass letter — N, S, E or W, a setter's usual meaning — and it is a prong instead, which is four letters rather than one.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant is somebody with no fixed home who moves from place to place, and the answer is the noun for exactly such a wanderer.

clue.text: Concluded special finish to exhaust

parts.note: when something is concluded it is over
standard abbreviation
a finish is an end

explanation.surface: A special race concluded with a finish that left the runners drained.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the three pieces mean 'end' — 'concluded' and 'finish' — which is what makes the clue read as one idea instead of three instructions in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust a fund is to use it all up and then some, and the answer is the verb for running through money past the point where any is left.

clue.text: The old boring mean settler

indicators.note: To bore into something is to drill into its middle, so the drilling word ends up inside the drilled one.

parts.note: par is the mean, the average, the standard figure
ye is the old way of writing 'the', as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe

explanation.surface: A dull, stingy old colonist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settler' looks like a colonist and 'mean' like stingy. Both are the wrong sense, and the surface is built so that the two wrong senses agree with each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a bill is to pay it, so 'settler' names the person doing the paying — a sense that survives mainly in accounts and in crosswords.

clue.text: Ruins potatoes?

parts.note: once 'Ruin' has been taken as the definition, the S left on the end of that word is the wordplay's first letter
mash is what boiled potatoes become

explanation.surface: A question about what ruins a potato.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'Ruins' is split down the middle: 'Ruin' is the definition and its final S joins the wordplay. Setters do that with a verb ending whenever the surface will carry it.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin something is to wreck it, and the answer is the blunter verb for the same act — breaking a thing apart beyond repair.

clue.text: Overexcited setter to noisily approach flowering plant

parts.note: hyper = overexcited
the person setting the clue calls himself I

indicators.note: Something done noisily is done out loud, so this piece reaches you as a sound and has to be respelt before it fits.

parts.note: to approach is to come, and that noise is spelt this way in words borrowed from Latin

explanation.surface: An overexcited red setter bounding noisily up to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is a gun dog on the surface and the clue's own author underneath. The plant is St John's wort, far better known by that name than by this one.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the botanical genus name of St John's wort, so 'flowering plant' is the general class the genus sits in.

clue.text: Expert ship's captain mostly occupied

parts.note: the master is the captain of a merchant ship

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, so its last letter is cut off

parts.note: a full room or seat is one that is occupied

explanation.surface: A skilled ship's captain who is busy most of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert' looks like it could describe the captain, but it is the definition, used as an adjective; the master of a merchant vessel is its captain.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterful means showing great skill, as an expert does, so the two are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Places that display musical boards?

parts.note: a musical is a show
to board somewhere is to room there, to lodge

explanation.surface: Somewhere with placards up advertising a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' looks like the theatre's own word — treading the boards — which keeps it inside the musical's world. It is the lodging verb instead.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Places that display' is a plain plural definition: the spaces a dealer lays stock out in for customers to walk round and look at.

clue.text: In favour of ex-president (Democrat), blocked and debarred

parts.note: to be for something is to be in favour of it

indicators.note: A blocked pipe has something stuck part-way along it, and that is where the blocking letter goes.

parts.note: Joe Biden, US president until January 2025
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A former US president, a Democrat, blocked and barred from something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blocked and debarred' reads as a single phrase, so the definition looks two words longer than it is. Only the last word of the clue defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To be debarred from something is to be shut out of it by rule, which is what the answer says as an adjective: not allowed.

clue.text: Liking the present, love? It's a starter

parts.note: somebody keen on now is set against what has gone: ANTI the PAST
love is a tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

explanation.surface: 'Do you like the present, love?' — somebody asking about a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is a parcel in the surface and an era in the wordplay, and 'love' is a term of endearment right up to the moment it turns into a nought.
explanation.definitionFit: A starter is the first course of a meal, and the answer is the Italian name for exactly that course.

clue.text: See 1
Alarm son accompanying trim Papas' woman

indicators.note: One thing accompanying another travels alongside it, so this letter is simply placed next to what follows.

parts.note: standard abbreviation
the first name of Irene Papas, cut short by a letter

explanation.surface: A son out walking with a trim woman of the Papas family.
explanation.walkthrough: Irene Papas was the Greek actress of Zorba the Greek and The Guns of Navarone. A surname pointing at a first name is a standard way of getting a common word out of a famous person.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm is the warning noise a device makes, and the answer names that wailing device on an ambulance roof or a factory wall.

clue.text: See 8
Coach tyres unable to operate reliably at the beginning

indicators.note: The phrase is about where to look rather than what to think: the opening letter of every word it governs.

parts.note: the initial letters of these five words, taken in order

explanation.surface: The tyres on a coach that will not work properly when it first sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' does two jobs: the bus the tyres belong to, and the person who teaches. It is the only word in the clue not lending a letter, which is what makes it the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To coach someone is to instruct them one to one, and the answer is the noun for the person who does that private teaching.

clue.text: Some barristers examine brief

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part rather than the whole, so what is wanted is a run of letters inside the words, not their meaning.

parts.note: five consecutive letters straddle the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Barristers going over a brief between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' is the barrister's bundle of papers on the surface and an adjective underneath, so both readings of the clue stay inside one profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief means short, and the answer is the adjective for speech pared to the minimum — few words, and a little curt with it.

clue.text: Lacking love, Chinese philosophy embraces yelling and uncontrolled dancing

indicators.note: embraces means holds within, so the philosophy wraps around the shouting
lacking means going without, so the letter for love is removed from the philosophy

parts.note: Taoism is the Chinese philosophy founded on the teachings of Laozi
O is love, a zero score in tennis
a rant is yelling or a loud tirade

explanation.surface: A school of Chinese thought, with no love left, takes up shouting and wild dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking love' removes the O from TAOISM to leave TAISM, which 'embraces' RANT. Tarantism was a dancing mania once blamed on a tarantula bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarantism was a hysterical urge to dance found in southern Italy, thought to come from a spider bite.

clue.text: Test introduction of tandoori bread in the Middle East

indicators.note: An introduction comes at the front, so what is taken is the opening letter of the word being introduced.

parts.note: the first letter of tandoori
bread is slang for money, and the rial is the currency of Iran and Oman

explanation.surface: The bread that comes out of a tandoori oven, of the kind eaten in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is money, not the naan a tandoori oven promises. Both food words in the surface are there to keep you thinking about dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Test' matches the answer's sense of a controlled try-out — a new drug or a vehicle put through its paces — and not the courtroom sense it also carries.

clue.text: Bottom part of horrid android's turned up

indicators.note: 'Part of' asks for a piece of the words themselves, so the letters come straight out of the text rather than out of the meaning.
This is a down entry, so 'up' means reading from the foot of the answer towards the top — the letters arrive the other way about.

parts.note: five letters in a row straddle the join between these two words

explanation.surface: The lower half of a horrible robot, tipped upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom part of horrid android' reads as one description of a robot's lower half, which is how 'part of' slips past as an instruction rather than as description.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom is the lowest point of a thing, and the answer is the astronomer's word for the point directly beneath you — the opposite of the zenith.

clue.text: Instrument associated with West African city and lake

parts.note: a maraca is the gourd rattle shaken in Latin American bands
the Ibo are a people of southern Nigeria

explanation.surface: A musical instrument with some West African connection.
explanation.walkthrough: Maracaibo is Venezuela's second city, standing on the great lake of the same name, so 'city and lake' is one word doing two jobs rather than two answers.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to both a Venezuelan city and the vast lake beside it, so one word answers 'city and lake' at once.

clue.text: Move out of the way of car

definitions.meaning: the verb: to swerve aside to avoid something
a make of American car, the second definition

explanation.surface: Stepping smartly aside to avoid a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one continuous action — a person avoiding a vehicle — and it is two separate definitions with nothing but 'of' holding them together.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to move sharply aside to avoid something; the same word is an American car marque, so 'car' defines by naming one make.

clue.text: Sounds right wearing underwear at first in hot baths

indicators.note: You put clothes on around yourself, so the piece that is wearing something finishes up inside it.

parts.note: the insulating long johns and vests worn against the cold

indicators.note: 'At first' is about position and not about letters: the piece it follows is placed at the front of the answer.

parts.note: pings are small sharp sounds
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: It sounds right to keep your underwear on, at least at first, in the hot baths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' wants to be a homophone instruction, the commonest trap in the language of these clues. It is a plural noun instead — the small noises a machine makes.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Hot baths' describes naturally heated pools people bathe in, which is what these are: water warmed underground and rising to the surface.
